title: I feel empty, and I don't know why
seoTitle: Why Do I Feel Empty? Depression, Faith, and What Helps
description: Feeling empty, numb, or tired of everything? What might be going on, what the Bible says, when to get help, and small steps for this week.
summary: For the hollow, numb, tired-of-everything feeling: what it might be, what Scripture says, and when to get help.
askedAs: What does the Bible say about depression
answer: You can't point to one thing that's wrong, and that may be the hardest part. What used to matter has gone flat. You're numb, or just tired of everything, going through the motions while something inside has gone quiet, and you keep asking yourself *what's wrong with me*. None of this means you're weak or that your faith has failed. Emptiness like this can grow out of grief, long exhaustion, a dry season with God, or depression, a real and treatable medical condition, and often out of more than one. It can change. If it has turned into thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988 now. If not, start small tonight: eat something, put the phone down and sleep, and tell one person tomorrow.
happening:
Emptiness is hard to explain because it isn't really a feeling. It's the absence of the ones you used to have. Food loses its taste, sleep either doesn't rest you or becomes the only place you want to be, and you laugh at the right moments with nothing behind it. The people you love seem out of reach even in the same room, and *fine* is easier to say than an explanation you don't have. Then a second weight settles on the first: *I have a good life, so why do I feel like this?* Many Christians carry a third: *if I really believed, wouldn't I have joy?*

Emptiness isn't one thing, and the differences matter because they call for different help. Ordinary sadness usually has a reason, and it lifts with rest and time. Grief is emptiness with a shape, the hollow where a person, a marriage, a job, or a friendship used to be, and it comes in waves. Burnout is a tank drained by too much for too long; it can feel like not caring when the truth is that you cared past your limit. Spiritual dryness is quieter: prayer goes flat and God feels far away, yet something in you still aches for him. The church has known that country for centuries; John of the Cross, a Spanish friar of the sixteenth century, wrote of one form of it as the dark night of the soul.

Depression is different again. When the flatness spreads to nearly everything (sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, the people and things you used to love) and stays most of the day, nearly every day, for two weeks or more, that is the pattern the National Institute of Mental Health says may be depression, and a persistent empty mood is one of the signs it lists. Depression is a real medical condition, it's common, and it's treatable. Some illnesses and medications can cause the same flatness, and these kinds of emptiness often travel together: grief can sink into depression, and exhaustion can make every prayer feel dry. If this sounds like you, see a doctor this week. You don't have to sort it out alone tonight.

Each common explanation gets something right. The medical account knows you're a body, and that a tired or sick body can make everything feel flat. Psychology understands how loss and old wounds bend the way we see. And the spiritual account knows we were made for God and can go dry. Taken alone, each leaves out the rest of you. God formed man from the dust and breathed into him, "and the man became a living being" (Genesis 2:7): dust and breath, one creature. So help has to reach all of you: bread and sleep and a doctor, honest prayer, and people who won't let you disappear.

scripture.intro: Scripture doesn't hurry past emptiness. Some of its most faithful people told God they wanted to stop living, and the Bible keeps their words without cleaning them up. These passages show a God who feeds the exhausted before he corrects them, gives words to people who have none, and lets hope be something you remember before you feel it.

passages.text: And Elijah was afraid and ran for his life. When he came to Beersheba in Judah, he left his servant there, while he himself traveled on a day’s journey into the wilderness. He sat down under a broom tree and prayed that he might die. “I have had enough, LORD,” he said. “Take my life, for I am no better than my fathers.” Then he lay down under the broom tree and fell asleep. Suddenly an angel touched him and said, “Get up and eat.” And he looked around, and there by his head was a cake of bread baked over hot coals, and a jar of water. So he ate and drank and lay down again. A second time the angel of the LORD returned and touched him, saying, “Get up and eat, or the journey will be too much for you.” So he got up and ate and drank. And strengthened by that food, he walked forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God.
passages.reading: Elijah had just seen fire fall from heaven on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18). One threat from Queen Jezebel, and he ran for his life, then asked God to take it, which is how despair talks: it makes no sense, and it sounds completely sure of itself. God doesn't rebuke him. He gives sleep, a touch, bread and water, more sleep, and a second touch, and the only reason the angel gives is the long walk still ahead. When the conversation comes, at Horeb, God answers Elijah's "I am the only one left" (1 Kings 19:14) with a companion and seven thousand others. God kept the man who asked to die alive, and fed him. If you're under your own broom tree tonight, eat something and sleep. And if you've had thoughts like his, tell someone tonight. You can call or text 988.

passages.text: I say to God my Rock, “Why have You forgotten me? Why must I walk in sorrow because of the enemy’s oppression?” Like the crushing of my bones, my enemies taunt me, while they say to me all day long, “Where is your God?” Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God.
passages.reading: The heading ties this psalm to the sons of Korah, a family of Levites who served in Israel's worship, and its writer remembers leading the procession to God's house with shouts of joy (verse 4). Now he's far from the temple, and people keep asking him, "Where is your God?" So he speaks to his own soul. "Why are you downcast, O my soul?" is a real question, and "Put your hope in God" is a direction he chooses to face while the feeling lags behind. He has asked it before (verse 5) and will ask it again (Psalm 43:5), because hope here is something you turn toward again, sometimes hour by hour. And he calls God "my Rock" and asks "Why have You forgotten me?" in one breath. You're allowed to pray both.

passages.text: But to You, O LORD, I cry for help; in the morning my prayer comes before You. Why, O LORD, do You reject me? Why do You hide Your face from me? From my youth I was afflicted and near death. I have borne Your terrors; I am in despair. Your wrath has swept over me; Your terrors have destroyed me. All day long they engulf me like water; they enclose me on every side. You have removed my beloved and my friend; darkness is my closest companion.
passages.reading: Psalm 88 is the darkest prayer in the Psalms, and it's there on purpose. Its heading names Heman the Ezrahite, and unlike most laments it never turns the corner into praise. It ends where he is: "darkness is my closest companion." God put a prayer with no happy ending into the songbook of his people, so if you can't make your prayer end well tonight, it's still a prayer. Notice what Heman keeps. He keeps talking, "in the morning my prayer comes before You," and he opens by calling God "the God of my salvation" (Psalm 88:1). He can't feel that salvation, but he says so to the One who holds it. Sometimes faith is simply refusing to stop talking to God.

passages.text: My soul has been deprived of peace; I have forgotten what prosperity is. So I say, “My strength has perished, along with my hope from the LORD.” Remember my affliction and wandering, the wormwood and the gall. Surely my soul remembers and is humbled within me. Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope: Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness! “The LORD is my portion,” says my soul, “therefore I will hope in Him.”
passages.reading: Some of the best-loved words about hope in the Bible were written while Jerusalem lay in ruins after Babylon burned it. The poet first says his hope is gone, "My strength has perished, along with my hope from the LORD," and three verses later writes, "Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope." The city is still rubble. What changes is what he calls to mind. Hope here begins as memory, choosing to remember who God has been when you can't feel who he is. "They are new every morning" is a promise sized to one day, mercy enough for this morning. When you can't feel hope, you can still remember. That's where this poet started.

whyHard:
Our culture has an answer ready for emptiness, and it usually comes as advice: *find your passion*, *chase your purpose*, change the job, build a better life. Some of that is true. People need work that matters and love that holds. But the advice assumes that meaning is something you produce, and that if you feel empty, you've failed to produce it. We've made meaning a do-it-yourself project, and when it won't stand, we blame the builder.

The philosopher Charles Taylor built *A Secular Age* (2007) around a question: how did the West go from a world, around 1500, where it was nearly impossible not to believe in God, to one where belief is one option among many? We now live inside what he calls the immanent frame, a world that can be explained on its own terms without reference to anything beyond it, and he describes a malaise that comes with it: meaning feels fragile, and ordinary days feel flat. That doesn't cause every emptiness; depression comes to believers too, in every century. I came to faith from atheism, and I won't tell you that people without God are secretly hollow. But when you're asked to be the source of your own meaning, a hard year can feel like a meaningless life, and no one was built to do a job only God can do.

We've also forgotten that we're bodies. We trade sleep for one more scroll and treat rest as a reward for work that never finishes, as if we were minds needing motivation rather than creatures needing sleep and bread and daylight. Scripture never made that mistake. "He gives sleep to His beloved" (Psalm 127:2), and God wrote a day of rest into the week, a command Deuteronomy ties to freedom from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15). A body denied rest for months will eventually tell the soul that nothing matters, and the soul will believe it.

Emptiness also grows best in private. Many of us have built lives in which no one would notice for weeks if we went quiet. Before Elijah lay down under the broom tree, he left his servant behind. Isolation follows emptiness, and then it feeds it.

And then there's us, the church. We should have been the one place where a person could say *I feel empty* out loud, and too often it had to be hidden there. We treated low mood as a shortage of joy or faith. We quoted "the joy of the LORD is your strength" (Nehemiah 8:10) at people who couldn't find any, though Nehemiah said it while telling a weeping crowd to go and eat, drink, and send portions to those who had nothing prepared. Those of us who preach have too often made the pulpit the last place a dark season could be admitted, and I'm a pastor, so I can't point at this from outside it. Yet Charles Spurgeon, the famous preacher of Victorian London, gave his students a lecture called *The Minister's Fainting Fits* in *Lectures to My Students*, telling them depression would come to most of them, speaking of his own, and describing a depression with no cause he could name. The church has known how to say this out loud before.

So the emptiness you're carrying is heavier than it has to be, and not all of the weight is yours. You can't will your way out from under it, and you were never meant to. Creatures aren't fixed by trying harder. They're fed, usually by someone else's hands.

thisWeek.intro: If you've had any thought of ending your life, the first step isn't on this list. Call or text 988 now, and tell someone near you. Otherwise, start with the smallest faithful thing. You don't have to do all of these or feel like doing any of them. Pick one for today.

steps.title: Eat a meal and get some sleep
steps.body: Start where God started with Elijah. Eat a real meal today, even a small one, and drink some water. Tonight, pick a bedtime and put your phone in another room; if you've been sleeping far too much, set one alarm and get up with it. It won't cure a deep emptiness, but it gives your body a floor to stand on, and a fed, rested body can hear what a hungry, sleepless one can't.

steps.title: Tell one person today
steps.body: Choose one person you trust and tell them the truth in a sentence: *I've been feeling empty for a while, and I don't want to carry it by myself.* You don't need to explain it or know why. If saying it aloud is too hard, text it. Emptiness grows in private, and one honest sentence to one person begins to break that.

steps.title: Call a doctor this week
steps.body: Call your doctor, or a clinic if you don't have one, and ask to be seen about how you've been feeling. Say how long it's been and what has changed: sleep, appetite, energy, focus, interest in what you used to love. Some physical conditions and medications cause this kind of flatness, and a doctor can check. Going is a way of caring for the body God gave you.

steps.title: Pray one honest sentence
steps.body: You don't need the right words or feelings. Tell God the truth in a sentence, something like *Lord, I feel nothing, and I'm telling You anyway.* If you have no words at all, read Psalm 88 or Psalm 42 aloud and let the psalmist pray for you. God has heard prayers like that before, and he kept them in his book.

steps.title: Walk outside for fifteen minutes
steps.body: Go outside in daylight and walk, even slowly, even just around the block. Movement and daylight won't fix everything, but they often help, because you're one creature, body and mind, and what happens to one reaches the other. Leave the headphones at home and look around you. If fifteen minutes is too much, walk to the mailbox and back. That counts.

steps.title: Keep one small appointment with your life
steps.body: Emptiness tells you to stop doing the things that used to connect you, then points to the silence as proof that nothing matters. Refuse it in one small way: sit in the back row at church, call an old friend, or play with your kids for ten minutes. You don't have to feel anything while you do it. Often the feeling comes back after the doing.

moreHelp.body:
Emptiness becomes more than a pastoral matter when it lasts, spreads, or turns toward death. If it has gone on for more than two weeks, if it's changing your sleep or appetite or your ability to work, or if you're drinking to get through it, see a doctor and a counselor. Depression is treatable, counseling helps many people, and if a doctor recommends medication, taking it is not a failure of faith. I'm a pastor, not a physician, and nothing here is medical advice.

To find a counselor, ask your doctor for a referral, check your insurance company's directory, or ask a pastor who knows the counselors nearby. If you want a Christian counselor, look for one who is also licensed, since the word Christian on a sign isn't a credential, and confirm any license with your state's licensing board. You don't have to be suicidal to call or text 988; it's there for anyone in emotional distress. If you're thinking about ending your life, don't wait for an appointment: call or text 988 now, or call 911 if you're in immediate danger.
signs: You've had thoughts of ending your life, or feel others would be better off without you. Call or text 988 now.
You or someone else is in immediate danger. Call 911.
The emptiness has lasted more than two weeks, most of the day, most days.
Your sleep or appetite has changed a lot, much more or much less than usual.
You can't keep up with work, school, or your family.
You're drinking or using drugs to get through the day.
Someone who knows you well has told you they're worried.
moreHelp.firstCall: You don't need a speech. You can say, *I've been feeling empty and flat for about a month, and it's affecting my sleep and my work. I'd like to be seen.* If you've had any thoughts of ending your life, say so plainly; they hear it often, and it helps them help you. Ask whether they take your insurance, what the first visit costs, and, with a counselor, whether they're licensed in your state. If your faith matters to you, it's fine to ask whether they're comfortable with that.
moreHelp.cost: Cost shouldn't be the reason you wait. A visit to your regular doctor is often covered by insurance, and 988 is free. Ask counselors about sliding-scale fees based on income. Community mental health centers offer reduced-cost care, university training clinics often charge less, and many employers have an employee assistance program with a few free sessions. And ask your church; some keep a fund for exactly this.

helping.body:
If someone you love has gone quiet, you may be seeing it before they can name it: pulling back from people, losing interest in what they loved, sleeping or eating very differently, saying they're tired of everything. Take it seriously without panicking. You don't have to fix it or explain it. Stay near, and keep the door open.

Some signs call for more than patience: talking about wanting to die, about being a burden, or about feeling empty with no reason to live; making a plan to end their life; pulling away from everyone; giving away things that matter to them; saying goodbye or putting their affairs in order. The National Institute of Mental Health names these among the warning signs of suicide. If you see them, ask directly: *Are you thinking about ending your life?* The same institute says asking does not put the idea in someone's head. If the answer is yes, don't leave them alone; call or text 988 together, or call 911 if they're in immediate danger.

Remember Job's friends. Their best work was the seven days they sat with him and said nothing (Job 2:13); the trouble began when they started to explain.
say: I've noticed you seem worn down. How are you, really?
You don't have to explain it. I just want to be with you.
Are you thinking about ending your life?
I'm bringing dinner Thursday. You don't have to talk.
Can I drive you to the doctor?
dontSay: You have so much to be thankful for.
helping.next: Come back after the first conversation; a text the next day tells them you meant it. Offer concrete help, a meal or a ride to the doctor, and bring in others so you're not their only support. If you're a teenager worried about a friend, tell a parent, a teacher, or a school counselor, even if your friend asked you to keep it secret; that's one secret no friend should keep. Scripture says "Carry one another's burdens" (Galatians 6:2), and it takes more than one of you.

prayer:
Lord, I don't feel much tonight, and I won't pretend with You. You already know.

What used to matter has gone quiet, and I can't tell You why. It may be my body, or grief, or tiredness, or a season when You've gone silent on purpose. You know. Help me find out.

You fed Elijah when he asked to die. You kept Heman's prayer in Your book, though it ended in the dark. So here is mine, the way it is.

Give me sleep, and bread I can taste. Put one person near me who won't leave, and give me the nerve to tell them the truth. If I need a doctor, don't let pride or fear keep me away. Keep me alive for the morning, and let there be a mercy in it, even one I can't feel yet.

You are my God when I can't feel it. I'm still talking to You. Let that be enough for tonight.

Amen.

faq.a: Yes. Faith doesn't make anyone immune to depression, any more than it makes them immune to diabetes. Elijah asked God to take his life (1 Kings 19:4). Paul wrote that hardships in Asia put him and his companions "under a burden far beyond our ability to endure, so that we despaired even of life" (2 Corinthians 1:8). Charles Spurgeon, one of the best-known preachers of his century, wrote openly about his own depressions. Being depressed is no sign that God has left you or that you never believed; you're a creature in a broken world, and creatures sometimes need a doctor.

No. Being depressed is not a sin, any more than a broken leg is, and deep sorrow isn't sin either: Jesus said, "My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death" (Mark 14:34), and he was without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Scripture does know that hidden guilt can weigh on a body (Psalm 32:3-4), and where that's part of the story, confession and forgiveness are real help. But assuming every darkness hides a sin was the mistake of Job's friends, and God told them, "you have not spoken about Me accurately" (Job 42:7).

faq.q: Is this the dark night of the soul, or depression?
faq.a: They can be hard to tell apart, and they can overlap. John of the Cross, a sixteenth-century Spanish friar, wrote of the dark night as a season when God withdraws the felt sweetness of prayer so a person learns to love him for himself. He also taught that not every dry season is that night, since dryness can come from sin, from lukewarmness, or from the body, and he allowed that what the medicine of his day called melancholy often deepened the night itself. So the body matters even here. If your sleep, appetite, energy, or concentration has changed, or you've lost interest in nearly everything, see a doctor, whatever else God may be doing, and talk with a pastor too. A dark night is never a reason to skip the doctor.

faq.q: Is it wrong for a Christian to take antidepressants?
faq.a: No, though whether they're right for you is a decision for you and your doctor. Some Christians worry that medication will numb the soul or cover a spiritual problem, and the worry comes from something good: we're more than chemistry. We aren't less than chemistry either, and the brain can get sick like any part of the body God made. Paul told Timothy to take a little wine "because of your stomach and your frequent ailments" (1 Timothy 5:23) and called Luke "the beloved physician" (Colossians 4:14). Medication doesn't replace prayer or the church, and it doesn't shrink your faith.

faq.q: Does God hear me when I can't pray?
faq.a: Yes. Prayer doesn't depend on how well you do it: "the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words" (Romans 8:26). The Psalms give you words when you have none; read Psalm 88 or Psalm 42 aloud and let them be your prayer. And let others pray for you. When Paul was under a burden he couldn't bear, he told the Corinthians they were helping him "by your prayers" (2 Corinthians 1:11). When you can't carry your own prayers, the church can carry them for a while.

faq.q: Will this feeling ever go away?
faq.a: I can't promise when, and I won't pretend to. But emptiness usually isn't permanent, even when it feels as if it always will be. Grief softens as it's carried, exhaustion yields to real rest, dry seasons end, and depression is treatable. Christian hope rests on something deeper than the feeling lifting. Paul, who had once given up hope of coming through alive, wrote that it taught him to trust "God, who raises the dead" (2 Corinthians 1:9), and he lived to write that God had brought him through. The last word belongs to the One who says, "Behold, I make all things new" (Revelation 21:5). Until then, his mercies come one morning at a time.

slots.note: If James has his own story of a season of emptiness, dryness, or depression, before or after he came to faith from atheism, and wants it told, a short paragraph in his own words would strengthen this section. The page stands without it.
As the father of five sons, James could add, in his own words, what he would want a parent to know when a child goes quiet or says nothing matters. The page stands without it.

sources.claim: Depression's symptoms last most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks, and a persistent empty mood is among its signs; some medical conditions and medications can cause the same symptoms.
sources.cite: National Institute of Mental Health, Depression

sources.claim: Warning signs of suicide include talking about wanting to die or about being a burden; feeling empty, hopeless, or without a reason to live; making a plan; withdrawing; giving away important possessions; saying goodbye; and putting affairs in order. Asking about suicide does not cause or increase suicidal thoughts.
sources.cite: National Institute of Mental Health, Frequently Asked Questions About Suicide

sources.claim: You do not need to be suicidal to contact 988; it also serves people in emotional distress.

Spurgeon's lecture The Minister's Fainting Fits tells his students that fits of depression come over most of them, speaks of his own (his experience on first becoming a pastor in London), and describes a causeless depression that cannot be reasoned with.
sources.cite: C. H. Spurgeon, Lectures to My Students, Lecture 11, The Minister's Fainting Fits

sources.claim: Charles Taylor's A Secular Age (2007) asks how the West moved from a world around 1500 where it was virtually impossible not to believe in God to one where belief is one human possibility among others, describes the immanent frame, and describes a malaise that comes with modern immanence, including the fragility of meaning and the flatness of the ordinary. The page paraphrases the idea and does not attribute a phrase to Taylor.
sources.cite: Charles Taylor, A Secular Age (Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2007); the malaise is treated in chapter 8, The Malaises of Modernity

sources.claim: In Book I of the Dark Night, John of the Cross describes God weaning beginners from the sweetness they found in prayer; in chapter 9 he gives signs for telling this dryness from dryness caused by sins and imperfections, weakness and lukewarmness, or a bad humour or indisposition of the body, and allows that melancholy or another humour may increase the purgative dryness (as it frequently does).
sources.cite: John of the Cross, Dark Night of the Soul, Book I, chapter 9

Kit: every label checked against its target; the plan label matches plans-index.json; the dark-night essay's real title is Not Every Darkness Is a Doctrine Problem, and the label is kept as an honest description of the question it answers. No statistics, no quotations but Scripture; first person only for conviction and stance; two slots left for James. Read as the midnight reader on a phone, the skeptic, a pastor, and a licensed counselor.
